subject: Architecture
title: The Millennium Tower: San Francisco's Sinking Skyscraper
description: Learn The Millennium Tower: San Francisco's Sinking Skyscraper in one minute.

hook.text: A luxury San Francisco skyscraper has sunk 18 inches and tilted 14 inches since it opened in 2009.

buildup.text: The 58-story Millennium Tower was built on friction piles driven 80 feet down — but not to bedrock 200 feet below.

discovery.text: Apartments sold for up to $10 million. Residents discovered the sinking from news reports, not from the developer.

twist.text: A $100 million repair plan drove new piles to bedrock. During the work, the building tilted slightly more.

climax.text: Lawsuits between the developer, the city, and the transit authority dragged on for years before settling.

punchline.text: A $350 million tower that skipped bedrock. Penny wise, pound sunk.

quiz.question: Why is San Francisco's Millennium Tower sinking?
options: Earthquake damage cracked the foundation in 2010
Its piles were driven only 80 feet, not to bedrock at 200 feet
Underground water erosion dissolved the concrete foundation

details.summary: San Francisco's 58-story Millennium Tower has sunk over 45 centimeters and tilted noticeably since its 2009 completion. Built on friction piles that don't reach bedrock, the luxury condo tower became the subject of lawsuits, engineering interventions.
details.whyItMatters: The Millennium Tower demonstrates that even in a modern, regulated city, foundation engineering mistakes can create billion-dollar problems. It exposed gaps in oversight of tall building foundations and triggered industry reform.
takeaways: The 58-story Millennium Tower has sunk over 45 cm since 2009
Friction piles that don't reach bedrock caused the settlement
It triggered lawsuits and foundation engineering reform

faq.question: Why is the Millennium Tower sinking?
faq.answer: Its foundation uses friction piles driven 24 meters into dense soil rather than reaching bedrock 60 meters below. The piles rely on skin friction with surrounding soil, which is consolidating under the tower's weight. Adjacent construction may have also accelerated settlement.

faq.question: Can the sinking be stopped?
faq.answer: A $100 million fix installed 52 new steel-and-concrete piles to bedrock along two sides of the building. The tilting has slowed dramatically, though full stabilization takes time. Lawsuits involving the developer, city, and transit authority have cost hundreds of millions more.
